1.1 Sanatana Dharma
‘Hinduism’ is a name given to Sanatana Dharma by western researchers. Our
religion originally had no name because, initially, it was the only one that existed.
Even the term ‘Sanatana Dharma’ is not an official name for our religion but it is a
term that means ‘eternal dharma’, because it is a dharma that always existed.
How did our religion then come to be called as Hinduism? According to historians,
every civilisation has grown along the banks of a river because people subsisted on
agriculture and maintenance of cattle. History refers to the civilisation that existed
along the banks of river Sindhu as ‘Indus Valley Civilisation’, ‘Indus’ being a later
variation of the name ‘Sindhu’. The people who lived along the river Sindhu were at
first called Sindhus. Over a period of time, the term morphed into Hindus, and thus
the term Hinduism came about.
With so much discussion on this term ‘Sanatana Dharma’, it is important that we as
Hindus understand the ‘literal’ meaning of Sanatana Dharma:
‘Sanātana'
-
traces its roots as ‘सदा भव’ (sadā bhava), which, after Samskrita grammar
treatments, becomes ‘Sanātana’.
-
Sanātana’ means that which exists (bhava) always (sadā); eternal, ever-present,
permanent, etc.
‘Dharma’
-
traces its root to the root verb ‘dhr’ meaning that which upholds, supports, or
maintains everything.
-
‘Dharma’ can also mean ‘an essential quality’ or ‘true innate nature’ of an entity.

1.2 Our Grand Shastras - Overview
• The authoritative texts which establish the true knowledge of Dharma are called
“Pramāṇas”. (Pramā means truth "as it is"; that which establishes this is
Pramāṇa.)
• The primary pramāṇa, supreme authority, are the "Vedas" (four branches). Apart
from the Vedas, there are 10 more texts which expand or supplement the Vedas,
making it 14.
• Add with appendices (four more), we have totally 18 first level Pramāṇas!
(These shall be discussed in the "Intermediate Level” course.)
Vedas (Means “Knowledge")
• This is considered to be the divine knowledge of Bhagavan Himself and
hence is the "root" of all creation.
• They are truly "infinite" — says the Vedas themselves.
• They are the “life breath” of Bhagavan.
• Bhagavan said in Srimad Bhagavad Gita: "I am known through all the Vedas.-
(vEdaishcha sarvai: ahameva vedya: -BG 15:15)
• A great Rishi (Āpastamba) said: "Vedas are the Pramāṇa of all Dharma."
Vedas are not a product of human intelligence! (Sanskrit term: Apauruṣheya)
• The pronounced sound of the Vedas is the key! The sound itself has creative
ability. It also encompasses grand divine meaning covering all facets of life.
If at all we need to point to one rishi in history as a rejuvenator of our Dharma, it is
Sage Veda Vyāsa (The divine incarnation of Bhagavan’s “Jnana”, born to Sage
Parāshara & Satyavati Devi)
Sage Veda Vyāsa codified the Vedas into 4 branches:
1. Ṛig — "Hymn in praise.” (Riks)
2. Yajur — "Worship with sacrifice"; ritualistic procedures.
3. Sāma — Means "peace to minds”; Riks set to music.
4. Atharva — Types of mantras to ward off evil/hardship (discovered by Rishi
named Atharvan)

Srimad Bhagavatam Certification Course — Session 1: Sanatana Dharma + Shastras + Puranas

"Others may have a holy book; ours is a huge library!" — H.H. Maharanyam Sri Sri Muralidhara Swamiji

'Sanātana' means "always (sadā)" or "that which exists (bhava)"; eternal, ever-present.
'Dharma' means "an essential quality" or "true innate nature" of an entity.

'Sanātana Dharma' is:
- Eternal, Universal, Cosmic Law — the natural order — one which can never be destroyed.
- An eternal "way of life" — codes of both internal and external conduct, ethics, and responsibilities.
- The path to realizing lasting happiness through aligning thoughts, speech, and action with Universal Values, in line with scriptures.

Quote: "vEdaishcha sarvai: ahameva vedya:" — Srimad Bhagavad Gita 15:15 — "I (Bhagavan) am known through all the Vedas."

Theme: inquiry > blind dogmas.

The Great Vedas: Any good path (shown by the Vedas), and followed with faith and loyalty, is supported for any devatā, to realize the true goal. The Vedas have 4 portions, likened to a tree:
1. Saṁhitā — Mantras (the trunk)
2. Brāhmaṇa — Rituals (the branch)
3. Āraṇyaka — Philosophy (the unripe fruit)
4. Upanishads — Knowledge (the fruit)

Our Grand Shastras — the Pramanas ("Truth as it is"), shown as a pyramid with Purānās as the widest base, Itihāsās in the middle, and Vedas at the top:
- Vedas (4 branches): means "knowledge"; divine knowledge, root of creation.
  - Rig — Hymn in Praise
  - Yajur — Worship with Sacrifice
  - Sāma — Peace to Minds (music)
  - Atharva — Mantras to ward off Evil
- Itihāsās (2):
  - Srimad Rāmāyanam — by Sri Valmiki Maharshi
  - Srimad Mahābhāratam — by Sri Veda Vyasa Maharishi
- Purānās (18): grouped by the Gunas (Sātvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa); each has a primary Deity/Focus.

The Puranas:
- 18 Puranas total, with 400,000 total verses combined.
- Grouped by Gunas; each Purana has a primary Deity/Focus.
- All 18 were written by Veda Vyasa, except the Vishnu Puranam.
- Sātvika group: Vishnu Puranā, Srimad Bhāgavata Puranā, Nārada Puranā.
- Rājasa group: Brahma Puranā, Brahmānda Puranā, Brahma-vaivarta Puranā.
- Tāmasa group: Matsya Puranā, Kurma Puranā, Linga Puranā.

Sage Veda Vyasa gave a synthesis of all Upanishads; harmonised them to show that
the message cut across all Upanishads is one and the same without any real conﬂict!
Sage Veda Vyasa gave this in the form of aphorisms (sutrās - short, distilled, concise

4 chapters

"Prastāna Traya" — The 3 Pillars of Sanatana Dharma's Philosophy, shown as a temple: the roof is Sanatana Dharma, and it rests on three pillars — Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, and Brahma Sutras.

1) Upanishads: the primary authority on highest truth, and comes from the Vedas. There are 108 mainstream Upanishads — 10 of them are considered the most important.
2) Srimad Bhagavad Gita: the divine discussion between Bhagavan Sri Krishna and Arjuna on the Kurukshetra battlefield. Part of the Mahabharata (Itihasa), and has 18 chapters and 700 slokas.
3) Brahma Sutras: a synthesis of all Upanishads by Sage Veda Vyasa to show that they all carry the same message. In the form of aphorisms (sutrās are short, concise rules).

"Srimad Bhagavatam is the essence of all three pillars!" How do we know this?
1) Upanishads (Vedas): Srimad Bhagavatam has a detailed commentary of the Gāyatri Mantra and contains the crux of all Upanishads.
2) Srimad Bhagavad Gita (Essence of Mahabharata): Srimad Bhagavatam is graced by the author of the Mahabharata himself, Sage Veda Vyasa, and is the essence of the Bhagavad Gita.
3) Brahma Sutras: Srimad Bhagavatam is the commentary of the Brahma Sutras, written by Sage Veda Vyasa himself — e.g. the first shloka of Srimad Bhagavatam expounds on the second Brahma Sutra.

Other specialities of Srimad Bhagavatam:
- It is the harmonized form (sāma roopa) of the Puranas.
- "Purānam Brahma Sammitam" (SB 1.3.40): Srimad Bhagavatam is equivalent to the Vedas.
- "Nigama kalpa tarōr galitam phalam" (SB 1.1.3): It is the fruit of all Vedas in a form accessible to all.

Srimad Bhagavatam is Bhagavan Himself:
- The Padma Purana describes the greatness of Srimad Bhagavatam in six chapters (the Srimad Bhagavata Mahatmyam).
  - The 3rd chapter of that Mahatmyam details a conversation between Sri Krishna and Uddhava.
- As Krishna is about to return to Vaikunta, Uddhava asks Him not to go, in order to protect His devotees from Kali Yuga.
- Krishna says that He shall remain on Earth in the form of Srimad Bhagavatam.

3.1  Being a Rasika

Here is a secret!
A Purana story can be embellished in three deeper levels
a) Dharma (Righteousness / Do’s & Dont’s / the underlying value)
b) Tattva (The underlying philosophical principle/tenet)
c) Rasa (The relish / aesthetic ﬂavor expressed ‘poetically’)
Great ones generally tell stories to all; dharma to thousand; tattva to ten and rasa to
one!
Srimad Bhagavatam is a rare Purana that is almost exclusively for Rasikas.
Let us be a Rasika by divine grace, to relish this journey the most!

Let us see these three narratives with reference to Srimad Bhagavata Mahatmyam
itself as an example:
a) Dharma narrative
“Listen  to  and  read  Srimad  Bhagavatam;  it  is  enough!  Chant  the  divine  name  of
Hari and be in a satsang as much possible. Four major Puranas speak extensively
about  the  greatness  (Mahatmya)  of  the  Srimad  Bhagavatam:  the  Skanda  Purana,
Padma Purana, Garuda Purana, and Naradiya Purana.”

bonnum of learning. As seen above, four major Puranas speak extensively about the
greatness (Mahatmya) of the Srimad Bhagavatam. Why?”

Padma Purana, which celebrates the greatness of religious vows (vrathas);

1. Atmadeva and his wife Dhunduli had everything, except a child. A great sanyasi gave them a divine fruit, but fearing pregnancy Dhunduli secretly fed it to their cow instead.

Three Types of Samhitas
1. The Vedas are known as ‘Rāja Samhita.’ The Vedas issue commands. They do
not coax or plead with us. They command us like a king, saying, “Speak the
truth; remain steadfast in dharma.” So, the Vedas are called the Rāja Samhita.
2. The Puranas are known as ‘Suhṛt Samhita.’ In Sanskrit, the word suhṛt means
‘friend.’ The Puranas explain spiritual truths to us in a friendly, kind, and
approachable manner—speaking in a way that can help us understand and
accept them. Hence they are called the Suhṛt Samhita. We already saw that
Puranas can be classified based on the three gunas: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.
Each Purana speaks in a manner suited to people of the corresponding
temperament and qualification. Srimad Bhagavatam is a sāttvika Purana. It
never threatens or intimidates. Instead, it presents the very same truths taught
by the Vedas in a delightful and appealing manner, thereby elevating us greatly.
3. Certain other sacred compositions are known as ‘Kāntā Samhita.’ These are
divinely inspired works of great poetic beauty, bestowed upon us by many
mahatmas. Just as a loving wife speaks gently, gracefully, and appropriately to
her husband, the Kāntā Samhita conveys spiritual truths with tenderness and
charm. Our Sri Swamiji’s Madhurageethams are Kāntā Samhitas graciously
bestowed especially for us.
What does ‘Purana’ mean?
‘Purana’ literally means ‘ancient’. It is sacred literature which is a compilation of
stories from ancient history. It covers a wide range of topics and presents abstract
concepts of the Vedas in an easily understandable form, through examples and
stories. There are 18 Puranas in all, as we saw earlier.

Srimad Bhagavatam Certification Course — Session 6: Canto 1, Chapters 2-6

Suta Pauranika begins answering the 6 questions put forth in the previous chapter (see Week 5); this session covers Sage Narada and Sage Veda Vyasa's conversation.

Chapters 2 & 3: True Dharma is only that which flowers Bhakti in our hearts — practices that do not lead to devotion are ultimately in vain.
- Mundane Practice: a cycle of Dharma → Artha → Kama → Enjoyment of senses → (back to) Dharma.
- Path shown by Srimad Bhagavatam: Artha → Dharma → Bhakti → Jnana → Ananda.
- The Supreme Reality can only be attained through Bhakti, and Satsanga awakens the desire for this devotion.
- Upon concisely answering the 6 questions, Suta Pauranika says that Srimad Bhagavatam itself is the answer to these questions.

Chapter 4: Sri Shaunaka Rishi asked Suta Pauranika 4 more questions about Srimad Bhagavatam:
1. When, where, and why was this discourse of Srimad Bhagavatam held?
2. Who inspired Sri Veda Vyasa to compose Srimad Bhagavatam?
3. How did Sri Shuka, an enlightened soul, come to learn this Purana from his father?
4. Why did King Parikshith renounce his kingdom and take a vow to fast unto death, and how did he get to meet Sri Shuka and listen to the Purana from him?

Suta Pauranika starts with the avatara of Sri Veda Vyasa: Sri Vyasa was born in the Dwapara Yuga to Satyavati and Sage Parashara. Upon seeing the plight of the people in Kali Yuga and feeling dissatisfied with all his works (other Puranas, Mahabharata, etc.), he was deeply disturbed and wondered what he could do to ease their suffering.

Chapters 5 & 6: As Sage Vyasa was feeling restless, Sage Narada arrived at his ashram. When Sage Vyasa asked Sage Narada to give him clarity on why he was feeling this way, Narada pointed out that none of the works he had authored thus far were dedicated to extolling the glories and leelas of Bhagavan. He then began telling Sage Vyasa the story of his own previous birth.

Narada Maharishi's Story:
- Sage Narada was born as the son of a maid in a village, and was blessed with the satsang of sadhus during their Chaturmasya vratha.
- His ears were filled with the glories of Bhagavan during their stay, and while leaving the village the Sadhus instructed him on the highest truth.
- Soon, Narada's mother passed away and he left the village and began to meditate on Bhagavan.
- Though he had a vision of Bhagavan for just a split-second, a divine voice told him that he was not yet ready and this vision was a blessing because of his service to the Sadhus.
- He spent the rest of his days chanting the names of the Lord, and in the next life was reborn as Sage Narada, son of Brahma.

"The purpose of any Dharma is to bring a deep desire to listen to Krishna Katha." — Srimad Bhagavatam

Krishna rushed to the tent of Draupadi and were shocked beyond words to witness
the gory scene. Arjuna vowed to bring to her the head of the perpetrator. Knowing
that it must have been none other than Ashwatthama, Arjuna and Lord Krishna set
out to catch him, who was by then running for his life. Frightened and cornered by
Arjuna  and  Krishna,  Ashwatthama,  in  desperation,  hurled  at  them  the  powerful
Brahmastra,  which  he  did  not  know  to  properly  control  or  wield.  Arjuna
surrendered  to  the  Lord,  seeking  His  guidance.  Bhagavan  instructed  Arjuna  to
counter  it  with  another  Brahmastra  and  retract  both  of  them.  Arjuna  did  so,  and
then bound Ashwatthama.
Lord Krishna tested Arjuna by asking him to kill Ashwatthama then and there. But
knowing  the  heart  of  Krishna,  Arjuna  refrained  from  killing  him  and  merely
dragged the bound Ashwatthama to the tent of Draupadi. Draupadi was shocked to
see that the perpetrator was Ashwatthama. Empathising with the pain of his mother
Krupi,  the  compassionate  Draupadi  requested  that  he  be  released.  Yudhishthira
agreed,  while  Bhima  countered  it.  Arjuna  looked  to  Krishna  again  and  Bhagavan
said,  “Do  that  which  would  please  all  the  parties  and  Me!”  Arjuna  insulted
Ashwatthama by cutting off the gem in his head and then let him go. The Pandavas
performed the funeral rites for their sons and relatives.

Arjuna had gone to Dwaraka to see his relatives and had not returned even though

The  noble  king  Parikshith  ruled  ably  over  the  earth.  He  married  King  Uttara
Kumara’s  daughter  Iravati  and  begot  four  sons.  Once,  during  his  conquests,  he
beheld a strange divine vision. He saw a cow that was shedding tears profusely as it
stood alongside a bull who was standing on only one leg, with its other three legs
having  been  broken.  The  bull  was  enquiring  as  to  why  the  cow  was  in  tears.  The
cow revealed that it was because the Lord had left her. Parikshith then saw a man
who looked like a rogue but who was disguised as a king, hurting the cow and bull.
Parikshith  addressed  the  man  angrily  and  asked  who  he  was,  and  also  asked  the
bull about who had cut off his three legs.

The four legs of Dharma are:
1. Tapas - austerity
2. Shaucham - purity
3. Daya - compassion
4. Satyam - truth.
Except satyam, all the other limbs of dharma (the bull) were broken.

The  bull  did  not  point  any  fingers  or  blame  the  man,  even  though  it  was  obvious
that  it  was  he  who  had  hurt  the  bull.  Parikshith  then  understood  the  bull  to  be
Dharma,  the  cow  to  be  Mother  Earth,  and  the  man  posing  as  a  king  to  be  Kali
Purusha. (When we gossip about the sinful activities of another, we get a portion of that sin.
Dharma avoided that! Hence Parikshith could discern that the bull was Dharma.)

When  Parikshith  was  about  to  kill  Kali  Purusha,  Kali  Purusha  fell  at  his  feet  and
surrendered.  Thus  Parikshith  refrained  from  killing  him,  and  provided  him  with
four  places  to  reside  -  gambling,  alcohol,  adultery,  and  violence  (falsehood,
intoxication, lust, and cruelty). When Kali Purusha requested for one more place -
Parikshith  gave  ‘gold’  (rajoguna)  as  the  5th  place  for  Kali  Purusha  to  stay.
Parikshith  then  restored  the  three  legs  of  Dharma  and  continued  to  rule  his
kingdom well.

Parikshith did not kill Kali Purusha and merely subdued him, even though this Kali
was literally a storehouse of evils, because he knew that in the Kali yuga, everyone
could  attain  Bhagavan  easily  through  the  path  of  Namasankirtana.  Another
‘positive aspect’ of the age of Kali is that good intentions, even if not translated to
action,  are  rewarded,  while  bad  intentions  are  not  punished  until  implemented
through action. Like a bee, Parikshith discerned this nectar (true essence) from the
flower (Kaliyuga) and let it be.
